claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) remains a considerable threat to human health.
source: TB, caused by Mtb remains a considerable threat to human health.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the global health impact of tuberculosis.

claim: In 2021, 10.6 million people fell ill with TB.
source: In 2021, 10.6 million people fell ill with TB, 1.6 million people died from the disease, and 450,000 new TB cases suffered from rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB on this globe (Bagcchi, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bagcchi, 2023.

claim: In 2021, 1.6 million people died from TB.
source: In 2021, 10.6 million people fell ill with TB, 1.6 million people died from the disease, and 450,000 new TB cases suffered from rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB on this globe (Bagcchi, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bagcchi, 2023.

claim: In 2021, 450,000 new TB cases suffered from rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB.
source: In 2021, 10.6 million people fell ill with TB, 1.6 million people died from the disease, and 450,000 new TB cases suffered from rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB on this globe (Bagcchi, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bagcchi, 2023.

claim: TB cure rates are insufficient due to the increasing emergence of drug resistance.
source: Although TB treatment measures are in place in many parts of the world, cure rates are insufficient due to the increasing emergence of drug resistance.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about TB treatment challenges.

claim: Novel intervention strategies against TB are urgently needed.
source: Therefore, novel intervention strategies are urgently needed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preceding discussion of drug resistance and insufficient cure rates.

claim: Mtb are engulfed by mononuclear phagocytes into the phagosome which matures and then fuses with lysosomes.
source: First, Mtb are engulfed by mononuclear phagocytes into the phagosome which matures and then fuses with lysosomes (Chandra et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chandra et al., 2022.

claim: PAMPs from Mtb are recognized by PRRs including TLRs, NLRs, CLRs and cGAS.
source: The pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) from Mtb are recognized by a variety of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), Nod-like receptors (NLRs), C-type lectins receptors (CLRs) and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS), resulting in production of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and anti-bacterial peptides to restrict bacterial growth (Reiling et al., 2002; Fremond et al., 2004; Wilson et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recognition of Mtb PAMPs by PRRs results in production of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and anti-bacterial peptides to restrict bacterial growth.
source: The pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) from Mtb are recognized by a variety of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), Nod-like receptors (NLRs), C-type lectins receptors (CLRs) and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS), resulting in production of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and anti-bacterial peptides to restrict bacterial growth (Reiling et al., 2002; Fremond et al., 2004; Wilson et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mtb can escape from the phagosome into the cytosol and can be recaptured in autophagosomes through xenophagy.
source: Mtb can escape from the phagosome into the cytosol and can be recaptured in autophagosomes, through a process termed xenophagy, to form a degradative autolysosome (Wang and Li, 2020; Lopez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang and Li, 2020 and Lopez et al., 2018.

claim: Cell-autonomous defense mechanisms include production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen intermediates, hypoxia, mild acidity, and nutrition deprivation.
source: Cell-autonomous defense mechanisms also include the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen intermediates, hypoxia, mild acidity, and nutrition deprivation (Nathan and Shiloh, 2000; Lupoli et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nathan and Shiloh, 2000 and Lupoli et al., 2018.

claim: Knowledge about host immune factors that target Mtb components and directly inhibit replication is limited.
source: However, our knowledge about host immune factors that target Mtb components and directly inhibit replication is limited.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Mtb can evade and resist immune defense by entering a state of dormancy which can last for years.
source: Mtb can evade and resist immune defense by entering a state of dormancy which can last for years.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mtb biology.

claim: Mtb dormancy is due to the capacity to synthesize a sturdy cell wall, slow down metabolism to promote growth arrest, and implement the stringent response.
source: This is due to the capacity of Mtb to synthesize a sturdy cell wall, slow down metabolism to promote growth arrest, and implement the so-called stringent response (Batt et al., 2020; Hauryliuk et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Batt et al., 2020 and Hauryliuk et al., 2015.

claim: The complex cell wall of Mtb provides a barrier for host defense and antibiotics.
source: The complex cell wall of Mtb provides a barrier not only for host defense, but also for antibiotics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the Mtb cell wall.

claim: Components of the Mtb cell wall are well-established drug targets.
source: Accordingly, components of the cell wall are well-established drug targets.
evidence: This is established knowledge in TB drug development.

claim: The essential core cell wall structure of Mtb is composed of peptidoglycan, arabinogalactan, and mycolic acids.
source: The essential core cell wall structure is composed of three distinct layers: (a) the cross-linked network of peptidoglycan (PGN), (b) the highly branched AG polysaccharide, and (c) the characteristic long-chain mycolic acids (Jankute et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jankute et al., 2015.

claim: AG has been an important target for anti-TB drugs.
source: Among these, AG has been an important target for anti-TB drugs, though understanding of its biological functions is limited.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TB drug targets.

claim: Ethambutol targets the arabinosyltransferases EmbA, EmbB, and EmbC, which are critical for AG synthesis.
source: E.g., ethambutol, one of the front-line anti-TB drugs, targets the arabinosyltransferases EmbA, EmbB, and EmbC, which are critical for AG synthesis (Escuyer et al., 2001; Goude et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Escuyer et al., 2001, Goude et al., 2009, and Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: It remains unclear whether AG is directly targeted by natural host immune factors in TB.
source: However, it remains unclear whether AG is directly targeted by natural host immune factors in TB.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: AG was identified as a virulence factor of Mtb that is recognized by galectin-9.
source: Recently, we identified AG as a virulence factor of Mtb that is recognized by galectin-9, a member of the β-galactoside binding gene family.
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' previous work.

claim: Upon AG binding, galectin-9 initiates the downstream TAK1-ERK-MMP signaling cascade leading to pathologic impairment of the lung.
source: Upon AG binding, galectin-9 initiates the downstream TAK1-ERK-MMP signaling cascade leading to pathologic impairment of the lung (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: Galectin-4 and galectin-8 directly kill E. coli by recognizing blood group antigens of bacteria.
source: Galectin-4 and galectin-8 directly kill E. coli by recognizing blood group antigens of bacteria (Stowell et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stowell et al., 2010.

claim: Galectin-9 impedes mycobacterial growth via its AG-binding property in a CRD2-dependent mode.
source: Here, we demonstrate a novel cell-autonomous mechanism by which galectin-9 impedes mycobacterial growth via its AG-binding property in a carbohydrate recognition domain (CRD) 2-dependent mode.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anti-AG IgG antibodies were identified in sera of TB patients.
source: Moreover, in sera of TB patients, we identified anti-AG IgG antibodies which were supposed to defend against TB.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anti-AG mAbs CL010746 and CL046999 restrain Mtb growth by regulating AG biosynthesis.
source: Employing a monoclonal antibody (mAb) screening array, we identified anti-AG mAbs, CL010746 and CL046999, which were capable of restraining Mtb growth by regulating AG biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AG possesses characteristic features of protective antigens.
source: Thus, AG possesses characteristic features of protective antigens.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about anti-AG antibodies inhibiting Mtb growth.

claim: Recombinant galectin-9 protein inhibits the growth of Mtb at a concentration as low as 10 ng/mL.
source: Real-time monitoring of in vitro cultures revealed that recombinant galectin-9 protein inhibits the growth of Mtb at a concentration as low as 10 ng/mL (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Native structural conformation of galectin-9 is required for its bacteriostatic effect.
source: Native structural conformation of galectin-9 was required for its bacteriostatic effect since heat inactivation at 95℃ for 5 min abrogated this activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Galectin-9 inhibited Mtb growth as validated by CFU assays.
source: CFU assays further validated that galectin-9 inhibited Mtb growth (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Galectin-9 impaired the replication of Mycobacterium smegmatis in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Galectin-9 also impaired the replication of the fast-growing Mycobacterium smegmatis in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The abundance of galectin-9 in serum from TB patients is profoundly higher than that from healthy donors.
source: Consistently, ELISA revealed a profoundly higher abundance of galectin-9 in serum from TB patients than that from heathy donors, implying that galectin-9 contributes to resistance against Mtb infection (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The average concentration of galectin-9 in the sera of healthy donors was 3.602 ng/mL.
source: Of note, the average concentration of galectin-9 in the sera of healthy donors was 3.602 ng/mL (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: High abundance of galectin-9 contributes to the maintenance of latent TB infection by restricting Mtb spreading from granuloma.
source: We speculate that this high abundance of galectin-9 contributes to the maintenance of latent TB infection by restricting Mtb spreading from granuloma, where the pathogen is contained.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed galectin-9 levels.

claim: Galectin-9 directly inhibits mycobacterial growth.
source: In sum, we conclude that galectin-9 directly inhibits mycobacterial growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Galectin-9 is recruited to mycobacteria in THP-1 cells in a time-dependent manner.
source: When human monocytic THP-1 cells were infected with Mycobacterium bovis BCG fused with DsRed, immunofluorescence assays revealed recruitment of galectin-9 to mycobacteria in a time-dependent manner (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: A robust accumulation of galectin-9 around invading Mtb H37Rv-GFP was observed in THP-1 cells post infection.
source: In line with this observation, a robust accumulation of galectin-9 around invading Mtb H37Rv-GFP was also observed in THP-1 cells post infection (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: Galectin-9 has been reported to be critical for initiation of mTOR signaling and induction of autophagy.
source: Though galectin-9 has been reported to be critical for initiation of mTOR signaling and induction of autophagy (Jia et al., 2018; Jia et al., 2020; Bell et al., 2021), our work revealed a novel cell-autonomous mechanism whereby galectin-9 recruitment restricts mycobacterial growth in an autophagy-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jia et al., 2018, Jia et al., 2020, and Bell et al., 2021.

claim: Galectin-9 recruitment restricts mycobacterial growth in an autophagy-independent manner.
source: Though galectin-9 has been reported to be critical for initiation of mTOR signaling and induction of autophagy (Jia et al., 2018; Jia et al., 2020; Bell et al., 2021), our work revealed a novel cell-autonomous mechanism whereby galectin-9 recruitment restricts mycobacterial growth in an autophagy-independent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Addition of lactose completely reversed mycobacterial growth inhibition by galectin-9 in vitro.
source: Addition of lactose rich in β-galactoside (generally used for neutralization of carbohydrate-binding of galectin-9) completely reversed mycobacterial growth inhibition by galectin-9 in vitro (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Addition of glucose had no effect on mycobacterial growth inhibition by galectin-9.
source: In contrast, the addition of glucose had no such effect (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The β-galactose binding property of galectin-9 is involved in mycobacterial activity.
source: These results indicate that the β-galactose binding property of galectin-9 is involved in mycobacterial activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lactose and glucose experiments.

claim: Addition of AG reversed growth inhibition by galectin-9.
source: Moreover, the addition of AG reversed growth inhibition by galectin-9 (Figure 2C), indicating that the AG-binding property of galectin-9 is involved in an anti-mycobacterial activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The AG-binding property of galectin-9 is involved in anti-mycobacterial activity.
source: Moreover, the addition of AG reversed growth inhibition by galectin-9 (Figure 2C), indicating that the AG-binding property of galectin-9 is involved in an anti-mycobacterial activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the AG reversal experiment.

claim: CRD2, but not CRD1, of galectin-9 mediated its interaction with AG.
source: Our previous work had demonstrated that CRD2, but not CRD1, of galectin-9, mediated its interaction with AG (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: Addition of purified CRD2, but not CRD1, hindered Mtb growth.
source: As expected, the addition of purified CRD2, but not of CRD1, to some extent hindered Mtb growth, emphasizing that AG binding to galectin-9 was sufficient for anti-mycobacterial effects (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: AG binding to galectin-9 is sufficient for anti-mycobacterial effects.
source: As expected, the addition of purified CRD2, but not of CRD1, to some extent hindered Mtb growth, emphasizing that AG binding to galectin-9 was sufficient for anti-mycobacterial effects (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CRD2 experiment.

claim: Carbohydrate recognition is essential for galectin-9-mediated inhibition of mycobacterial growth.
source: Taken together, carbohydrate recognition is essential for galectin-9-mediated inhibition of mycobacterial growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in Figure 2.

claim: An ELISA assay was developed for the identification of anti-AG antibodies by coating AG on plates.
source: An ELISA assay was developed for the identification of anti-AG antibodies by coating AG on plates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes a method developed in the study.

claim: There is a linear correlation between OD450 and serum dilution over an appropriate range.
source: An adequate window of serum dilutions allowed a linear correlation between OD450 and dilution over an appropriate range (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is a significant increase in the abundance of anti-AG antibodies among TB patients when compared to healthy donors.
source: Our findings revealed a significant increase in the abundance of anti-AG antibodies among TB patients when compared to healthy donors (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: During Mtb infection, anti-AG IgG antibodies are induced, which potentially contribute to protection against TB by directly inhibiting Mtb replication.
source: We speculate that during Mtb infection, anti-AG IgG antibodies are induced, which potentially contribute to protection against TB by directly inhibiting Mtb replication albeit seemingly in vain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed antibody levels.

claim: An antibody chip comprising 62,208 mAbs was developed to screen for anti-AG activity.
source: Given the high affinity between galectin-9 and AG, we developed an antibody chip comprising 62,208 mAbs to screen for anti-AG activity (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a method developed in the study, with a citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: 12 candidate mAbs exhibiting binding affinity to AG were filtered out.
source: We filtered out 12 candidate mAbs exhibiting binding affinity to AG (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: ELISA assay revealed a robust AG-binding curve for CL010746 (mAb1) and CL046999 (mAb2).
source: The ELISA assay revealed a robust AG-binding curve for CL010746 (referred to as mAb1) and CL046999 (referred to as mAb2) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Both mAb1 and mAb2 exhibited specific binding to Mtb H37Rv-GFP as demonstrated by immunofluorescent assay.
source: Furthermore, both mAbs exhibited specific binding to Mtb H37Rv-GFP as demonstrated by immunofluorescent assay (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: Anti-AG mAbs have been successfully developed that bind Mtb directly.
source: Therefore, we have successfully developed anti-AG mAbs that bind Mtb directly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Both mAb1 and mAb2 demonstrated inhibition of Mtb growth.
source: Both mAb1 and mAb2 demonstrated inhibition of Mtb growth (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Inhibition of Mtb growth by mAb1 and mAb2 was confirmed through CFU determination.
source: This finding was further confirmed through CFU determination (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both mAb1 and mAb2 markedly inhibited the growth of Mycobacterium smegmatis.
source: Likewise, both mAbs markedly inhibited the growth of Mycobacterium smegmatis as evidenced by real-time OD monitoring (Figure 5C) and CFU assay (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Anti-AG mAbs demonstrate direct blockade of mycobacterial growth through binding to AG.
source: In conclusion, the newly identified anti-AG mAbs demonstrated direct blockade of mycobacterial growth through binding to AG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Direct inhibitory effects on Mtb growth by anti-AG antibodies emphasize that AG expresses features of protective antigens.
source: Direct inhibitory effects on Mtb growth by anti-AG antibodies emphasize that AG expresses features of protective antigens.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: GO enrichment analysis revealed significant enrichment of numerous cellular and metabolic processes related to biosynthesis of the outer membrane upon treatment with anti-AG mAb1.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed significant enrichment of numerous cellular and metabolic processes, primarily related to the biosynthesis of the outer membrane, upon treatment with anti-AG mAb1. These processes include cell periphery, external encapsulating structure, organic substance metabolic process, cellular metabolic process, primary metabolic process, nitrogen compound metabolic process, and biosynthetic process (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The formamidopyrimidine-DNA glycosylase N-terminal domain was enriched based on the analysis of functional enrichment and protein domain of differentially expressed antigens.
source: Moreover, the formamidopyrimidine-DNA glycosylase N-terminal domain was enriched based on the analysis of functional enrichment and protein domain of differentially expressed antigens (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: KEGG pathway analysis demonstrated a significant enrichment of lipoarabinomannan (LAM) biosynthesis pathways.
source: Additionally, the KEGG pathway analysis demonstrated a significant enrichment of lipoarabinomannan (LAM) biosynthesis pathways (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The upregulated proteins Rv0236.1 and Rv3806c were involved in the biosynthesis of the mycobacterial cell wall arabinan.
source: Consistently, the upregulated proteins Rv0236.1 and Rv3806c were involved in the biosynthesis of the mycobacterial cell wall arabinan (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Rv0236c is predicted to be a cognate of the GT-C superfamily of glycosyltransferases and likely acts as arabinofuranosyltransferase involved in AG synthesis.
source: Rv0236c is predicted to be a cognate of the GT-C superfamily of glycosyltransferases and likely acts as arabinofuranosyltransferase involved in AG synthesis (Skovierová et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Skovierová et al., 2009.

claim: Rv0236A is a small secreted protein involved in cell walls and cell processes.
source: On the other hand, Rv0236A is a small secreted protein involved in cell walls and cell processes (Marmiesse et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marmiesse et al., 2004.

claim: Rv3806c is a decaprenylphosphoryl-5-phosphoribose (DPPR) synthase involved in AG synthesis.
source: Additionally, Rv3806c is a decaprenylphosphoryl-5-phosphoribose (DPPR) synthase involved in AG synthesis (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2015.

claim: Anti-AG mAbs regulate AG biosynthesis.
source: These data provide compelling evidence to suggest that anti-AG mAbs regulate AG biosynthesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the proteomic data.

claim: mAb1 and mAb2 treatment both led to a dispersed distribution of Mtb in cultures.
source: Intriguingly, mAb1 and mAb2 treatment both led to a dispersed distribution of Mtb in cultures (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Acid-fast staining revealed the formation of a cord-like structure in Mtb treated with mAb1 or mAb2.
source: Acid-fast staining further revealed the formation of a cord-like structure in Mtb treated with mAb1 or mAb2, which was not observed following ethambutol (EMB) treatment (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Anti-AG mAbs treatment markedly increased the thickness of the Mtb cell wall.
source: Moreover, electron microscopy demonstrated that anti-AG mAbs treatment markedly increased the thickness of the Mtb cell wall (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Targeting AG by specific antibodies, and likely by galectin-9 as well, impairs the growth of Mtb and other mycobacteria by modulating cell wall structure.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that targeting AG by specific antibodies, and likely by galectin-9 as well, impairs the growth of Mtb and other mycobacteria by modulating cell wall structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological characterization experiments.

claim: Galectin-9 and anti-AG antibodies serve as immune factors that restrain bacterial growth by targeting AG in the cell wall.
source: We conclude that galectin-9 and anti-AG antibodies serve as immune factors that restrain bacterial growth by targeting AG in the cell wall.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Increasing evidence suggests a role for antibodies in protection against TB.
source: Increasing evidence suggests a role for antibodies in protection against TB (Lu et al., 2019; Irvine et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lu et al., 2019 and Irvine et al., 2021.

claim: It is generally assumed that the role of antibodies in TB is based on their interactions with macrophages, which promote anti-mycobacterial activities.
source: It is generally assumed that the role of antibodies in TB is based on their interactions with macrophages, which promote anti-mycobacterial activities such as phagolysosome fusion and production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen intermediates (Chandra et al., 2022; Nathan and Shiloh, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chandra et al., 2022 and Nathan and Shiloh, 2000.

claim: Anti-AG antibodies directly impair Mtb growth.
source: In striking contrast, our findings demonstrate that anti-AG antibodies directly impair Mtb growth and thus emphasize that AG comprises features of protective antigens.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Fifteen different types of galectins are known in humans.
source: Fifteen different types of galectins are known in humans, which can be classified based on their structure, subcellular localization, and function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about galectins.

claim: Galectin-1 participates in regulating cell proliferation, apoptosis, and immune responses through interactions with specific glycosylated receptors on the cell surface.
source: For instance, galectin1 participates in regulating cell proliferation, apoptosis, and immune responses through interactions with specific glycosylated receptors on the cell surface, such as integrins and CD45 (Cedeno-Laurent et al., 2012; Perillo et al., 1995; Ge et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cedeno-Laurent et al., 2012, Perillo et al., 1995, and Ge et al., 2016.

claim: Galectin-4 disrupts bacterial membranes and kills E. coli through interactions with lipopolysaccharides on the bacterial outer membrane.
source: More recently, it was shown that galectin-4 disrupts bacterial membranes and kills E. coli through interactions with lipopolysaccharides on the bacterial outer membrane (Stowell et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stowell et al., 2010.

claim: Galectin-9 significantly inhibits the replication of Mtb by interacting with AG in Mtb via its CRD2 domain.
source: Here, we demonstrate that galectin-9 significantly inhibits the replication of Mtb by interacting with AG in Mtb via its CRD2 domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Galectin-4, galectin-6, and galectin-8 comprise 2 CRDs in tandem connected by a linker sequence.
source: Similar to galectin-9, galectin-4, galectin-6, and galectin-8 also comprise 2 CRDs in tandem connected by a linker sequence (Leffler et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leffler et al., 2002.

claim: After phagocytosis by pulmonary macrophages, Mtb downregulates its metabolism and enters a non-replicating persistent (NRP) state, termed dormancy.
source: After phagocytosis by pulmonary macrophages of the newly infected host, Mtb ends up inside phagosomes, where it downregulates its metabolism and enters a non-replicating persistent (NRP) state, termed dormancy, in response to host stress (Russell, 2001; Gengenbacher and Kaufmann, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Russell, 2001 and Gengenbacher and Kaufmann, 2012.

claim: Once the immune response 'breaks down,' Mtb transits into a metabolically active and replicative state which ultimately results in progression to active TB disease.
source: Once the immune response 'breaks down,' Mtb transits into a metabolically active and replicative state which ultimately results in progression to active TB disease (van der Wel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van der Wel et al., 2007.

claim: Galectin-9 accumulates around invading mycobacteria in host cells.
source: We demonstrated that galectin-9 accumulates around invading mycobacteria in host cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: AG is hidden by mycolic acids in the outer layer of Mtb.
source: Of note, AG is hidden by mycolic acids in the outer layer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mtb cell wall structure.

claim: During Mtb replication, cell wall synthesis is active and AG becomes exposed, thereby facilitating its binding to galectin-9 and leading to Mtb growth arrest.
source: We speculate that during Mtb replication, cell wall synthesis is active and AG becomes exposed, thereby facilitating its binding to galectin-9 and leading to Mtb growth arrest.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis by targeting InhA enzyme.
source: For instance, Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis by targeting InhA enzyme (Quémard et al., 1995), Ethambutol blocks AG biosynthesis by targeting EmbCAB complex Telenti et al., 1997, and Pyrazinamide disrupts the pH balance within the bacterial cell, thereby impairing mycobacterial growth (Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Quémard et al., 1995.

claim: Ethambutol blocks AG biosynthesis by targeting EmbCAB complex.
source: For instance, Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis by targeting InhA enzyme (Quémard et al., 1995), Ethambutol blocks AG biosynthesis by targeting EmbCAB complex Telenti et al., 1997, and Pyrazinamide disrupts the pH balance within the bacterial cell, thereby impairing mycobacterial growth (Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Telenti et al., 1997.

claim: Pyrazinamide disrupts the pH balance within the bacterial cell, thereby impairing mycobacterial growth.
source: For instance, Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis by targeting InhA enzyme (Quémard et al., 1995), Ethambutol blocks AG biosynthesis by targeting EmbCAB complex Telenti et al., 1997, and Pyrazinamide disrupts the pH balance within the bacterial cell, thereby impairing mycobacterial growth (Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 1999.

claim: To date, drugs that directly bind AG and inhibit Mtb growth have not been reported.
source: Although the mycobacterial cell wall has been widely exploited as an antibiotic target, to date, drugs that directly bind AG and inhibit Mtb growth have not been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Host galectin-9 and anti-AG antibodies recognize AG and thus inhibit Mtb replication.
source: Here, we identified host galectin-9 and anti-AG antibodies (both serum antibodies from patients and mAbs) which recognize AG and thus inhibit Mtb replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Anti-AG mAbs can be harnessed for the design of novel biologics which address the challenge of drug resistance in TB.
source: Hence, anti-AG mAbs can be harnessed for the design of novel biologics which address the challenge of drug resistance in TB.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Elevated levels of galectin-9 in the serum of active TB may be an indicator of the host immune response to Mtb infection.
source: We consider that the elevated levels of galectin-9 in the serum of active TB may be an indicator of the host immune response to Mtb infection, however, the magnitude of elevated galectin-9 is not sufficient to control Mtb infection and maintain latent infection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claim: The magnitude of elevated galectin-9 is not sufficient to control Mtb infection and maintain latent infection.
